https://www.dw.com/en/russia-announces-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5M6VQ Germany's St. Petersburg consulate will be closed down from September 18 Image: Olga Maltseva/AFP Advertisement The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg. The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 at the latest, according to the Foreign Ministry. "It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences. Russia also earlier ordered the closure of all Goethe-Institut branches on Russian territory, with Goethe-Institut staff having to leave the country by September 13. Goethe-Institut is a center that promotes German language and culture. Goethe-Institut is largely financed by the German government. Germany, Russia trade barbs over Leipzig drone attack The moves are a direct response to Germany's decision to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin , a decision Russia labeled "unfriendly." Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EU, too, said the incident had all the signs of "state sponsored terrorism." The Leipzig airport is an important international freight hub, also used for providing support to Ukraine. Russia Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejected Germany's allegations, calling them "the beginning of a real war." Edited by: Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Residents sit in front of a Kramatorsk apartment block damaged by a Russian strike By Vitaly Shevchenko Chief analyst, BBC Monitoring Published 11 September 2026, 00:22 BST It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region. In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police. "This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much. "If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day." Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" â a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east. However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it. The full capture of Donbas, made up of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is a key objective for Russia. Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Russian army already controls almost all of Luhansk region, and is now in control of almost 80% of Donetsk region too, where all three fortress cities lie. For the past few months, the territory near Kramatorsk and Slovyansk has been the main focus of Russian ground assaults. Capturing them would potentially make it much easier for Russia to advance to the west. The two cities are now facing intense strikes from drones and bombs. Many civilians have already left, and key streets there are now covered with anti-drone nets, says Viktor Makurin, a volunteer from London. "There are often [remote-controlled] FPV drones in the air, you can hear them through the window. Driving around the city is lethally dangerous. There are drones lying in ambush on the roads, too," he told the BBC. "You can always hear explosions in the background, plus there are mobile groups firing at drones." Image source, Reuters Image caption, Many of Kramatorsk's key streets are now covered with anti-drone netting Over the summer, the number of civilians wounded by Russian attacks on the two cities increased from 70 in June to 212 in August, say Ukrainian police. Sixteen people died in June, 20 in July and 15 in August. Residential housing comes under attack as well as infrastructure, says Dyachenko, causing "very significant destruction". The number of glide bombs launched by Russia jumped from 40 in June to 109 in July and 92 in August, according to data published by Ukrainian police and studied by the BBC. One morning two weeks ago, on 25 August, nine glide bombs targeted Kramatorsk. Seven hit civilian apartment blocks, wounding 24 people including a two-month-old baby, Ukrainian police say. Two days later, it was hit again, this time with seven glide bombs, and five bombs targeted Slovyansk. Fitted with winglets so they can glide to their target rather than fall, glide bombs are considered one of the most effective and lethal weapons in Russia's arsenal. Usually, they weigh 250 or 500 kg, but there have been cases of Russia deploying bombs that weigh 1,500 kg. "The devastation they cause is simply incredible," says Dyachenko. "Glide bombs are the big fear," another British volunteer, John Auckland Abbey, posted on social media. "They are silent killers, and when you've been abruptly woken by one exploding, you know at least another one will follow. The question you ask yourself as you lie very still in the dark is: will the next one be closer?" Image source, EPA Image caption, Seven people were wounded when Kramatorsk came under fire on Thursday Kramatorsk is currently home to the headquarters of the Donetsk regional administration. The capital city used to be Donetsk, until it was captured in 2014 by Russian-backed separatists. What happens to the areas of Donbas still under Ukrainian control was reportedly a key issue when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend after their talks with Putin. In the past, Witkoff has appeared to back Russian claims to the region, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is refusing to pull troops out of it. He says Putin has given his generals until the end of the year to complete their occupation of Donbas. "Putin's primary objective on the front line remains the same: Kostyantynivka-Slovyansk," Zelensky told journalists last month. Faced with mounting military pressure, the Ukrainian leader has created two new taskforces headed by experienced generals, Andriy Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, to defend the portion of Donbas still in Ukrainian hands. "There isn't just a battle for Donbas there," one unnamed Ukrainian general has said. "What is probably the main battle of this year and the next is now unfolding." https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/horror-wa.text: Olivia Beeson Updated Fri, September 18, 2026 at 2:23 AM UTC 0 Putin has issued a horror warning according to the Polish leader (Image: Getty) A horror warning that Putin could be planning to bomb the UK has been issued as NATO is placed on red alert. Poland's Prime Minister revealed on Thursday evening that Russia is preparing to launch missile strikes on countries supporting Ukraine. Donald Tusk issued the warning of wider conflict after the country was forced to close its airspace and airports due to the Kremlin's attack. He confirmed to parliament that Western intelligence agencies have verified Putin's plans to launch further attacks. Britain is likely to be among the countries Russia plans to strike as a key ally of Ukraine, the Mail reports. Mark Rutte, NATO chief, said that the UK needs a 'credible path' towards hitting its defence spending target with 'yearly increments'. If Russia were to launch missile strikes over British bases this would represent a significant escalation of conflict. Russian drone strikes and reconnaissance missions inside NATO airspace have occurred before but not missile strikes. The air strike in Poland came just days after a railway station close to the border was nearly struck by a high-speed jet-powered drone with Western dignitaries including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson on board. Tusk told Polish parliamentarians: "We know he is plotting something bad. However, for us the most important task is to prepare for various scenarios. "We will certainly not naively accept such messages that Russia has goodwill and will start behaving properly. There is no indication of this." Donald Tusk issued the warning after Poland were forced to close its airspace (Image: Getty) Tusk continued to add that intelligence was 'very consistent and convincing' and warned Russia could portray future attacks as incidental. He also added that Russia is looking to test NATO's resolve as never before over the coming months. As Russia increase their use of jet-powered drones in western Ukraine, there have been calls for Britain and other allies to shoot them down before they reach NATO airspace. Ben Wallace, former UK Defence Secretary described the move as 'the next natural step'. Tusk added: "There is a real risk that drones or other types of missiles could penetrate the territory of one or more countries on the eastern flank and even cause damage, while the official explanation will be that there was an accident." https://www.dw.com/en/poland-protesters-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OtEg Prefer DW on Google Donald Tusk's center-left governing alliance had vowed to reverse controversial PiS judicial reforms Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP Advertisement Protesters have gathered outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw since Friday evening, accusing Prime Minister Donald Tusk's center-left government of undermining the constitution and the judiciary after the court's president and deputy were suspended. The protests follow a statement published on the Constitutional Tribunal's website announcing that its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and his deputy had been suspended for one month . Fellow judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska will lead the court during that period. According to Warsaw police, officers responded to one judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff. Standoff over Poland's constitutional court escalates To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Tusk vows to 'restore rule of law' Swieczkowski is one of a slew of politically aligned judges who were appointed by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move in a post on X. "Restoring the rule of law is our duty," Tusk said. "After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added. When Tusk's center-left alliance took over after the 2023 parliamentary election, the group announced it would reverse controversial PiS government reforms in the judiciary. Riot police deployed to court Dozens of riot police were deployed to the court as followers of PiS protested against the ousting of Swieczkowski through the evening. Officers responded to a judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP The court's official X social media account said there had been a "coup d'etat," with some chanting "Tusk traitor" as they condemned the step taken by the Tusk government. Polish president discusses Constitutional Court row with politicians Meanwhile, President Karol Nawrocki began consultations with political representatives on Saturday amid the escalating dispute. The first to arrive at the Presidential Palace was Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the Christian-conservative Polish People's Party (PSL), which is part of Tusk's governing coalition. "State security, respect for democracy, social peace and public order are fundamental values," Kosiniak-Kamysz posted on X ahead of the meeting. He said these would be the issues he intended to discuss with the president. What is the dispute over the Constitutional Court? At the heart of the dispute is a power struggle between Poland's two largest political camps over control of the Constitutional Court. During its time in government, the nationalist-conservative PiS party appointed judges seen as politically aligned with it, reshaping the court's composition. The European Court of Justice subsequently ruled that the Constitutional Court could not be considered an independent and impartial tribunal because of serious irregularities in the appointment of some of its judges and its then president. In recent months, President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in five judges nominated by parliament. The judges instead took their oaths before parliament, but Constitutional Court president Bogdan Swieczkowski refused to grant them access to the court building.
